citation: Makransky, G., & Petersen, G. B. (2021). The Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL): A theoretical research-based model of learning in immersive virtual reality. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 937–958. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09586-2
thesis: CAMIL synthesizes the IVR-learning literature into the field's first research-based theoretical model, staking a 'media interacts with method' position between Clark's media-vehicles view and McLuhan's medium-is-message view: instructional methods validated on less-immersive media generalize to IVR, but certain methods become specifically more effective in IVR because they facilitate its two general psychological affordances — presence and agency — which arise from immersion, control factors, and representational fidelity, and which drive six affective/cognitive factors (interest, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, self-regulation) toward factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge acquisition and transfer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates a synthesizing theory for the rapidly growing but atheoretical IVR-learning literature, citing Radianti et al. 2020 (ped-sec-22) and Wu et al. 2020 as diagnosing the theory gap; introduces CAMIL as the remedy.

sections.title: Defining Immersive Virtual Reality
sections.summary: Defines VR (Mikropoulos & Natsis) and distinguishes IVR (HMD/CAVE, high immersion, objective per Cummings & Bailenson) from desktop/low-immersion VR; identifies immersion and interaction as the features separating IVR from video/PowerPoint and desktop VR.

sections.title: The Theoretical Perspective of CAMIL
sections.summary: Situates CAMIL within the media-vs-methods debate (Clark 1994 vs Kozma 1994 vs McLuhan 1964); proposes 'media interacts with method,' illustrated with three 2x2 studies (Meyer et al. 2019 N=118 pre-training x media; Makransky et al. 2020a N=165 enactment x media; Klingenberg et al. 2020 N=89 teaching x media) each showing a media-by-method interaction favoring IVR.

sections.title: General Overview of the CAMIL
sections.summary: States the model's four core claims and previews the path structure (Fig. 2): technological factors -> presence/agency -> six affective-cognitive factors -> learning outcomes; built directly on Lee, Wong & Fung (2010) and the cluster's own ped-sec-09 and ped-sec-11 SEM studies.

sections.title: What Factors Lead to Presence? / What Factors Lead to Agency?
sections.summary: Presence (Ijsselsteijn & Riva; Sheridan 1992) driven by immersion, control factors (Witmer & Singer, ped-sec-02), and representational fidelity (Dalgarno & Lee, ped-sec-04, cited as '2010'); three presence dimensions (physical, social, self; Lee 2004). Agency (Moore & Fletcher) driven primarily by control/fidelity of movement-feedback correspondence (Kilteni et al.; Farrer et al. forward-modeling/CNS account).

sections.title: How Do Presence and Agency Influence the Six Affective/Cognitive Factors?
sections.summary: Walks path-by-path through situational interest (Hidi & Renninger), intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan's SDT; Pekrun's CVTAE; Mayer's social agency theory), self-efficacy (Bandura; Schunk & DiBenedetto), embodiment (Kilteni et al.; Biocca & Frank; Gonzalez-Franco & Peck), cognitive load (Sweller's CLT; Mayer's CTML; Moreno & Mayer's seductive-details/extraneous-load research — presence and agency both positively predict extraneous cognitive load), and self-regulation (Boyd et al.; Zimmerman; Van Der Heijden's hedonic-systems framing; direction contingent on instructional design).

sections.title: Learning Outcomes (Factual/Conceptual, Procedural, Transfer)
sections.summary: Defines the outcome taxonomy (after Anderson et al. 2001) plus transfer (Perkins & Salomon); reviews mixed media-comparison findings (Parong & Mayer 2018 = ped-sec-08; Makransky et al.'s presence-but-less-learning study = ped-sec-10; Webster 2016) and links each of the six factors to outcome paths, including cognitive load's uniquely negative path.

sections.title: Implications for Future Research / Instructional Design
sections.summary: Recommends interaction-focused (not media-comparison) research designs; flags the hype/novelty effect (Fenn & Blosch; Clark 1983); for design, recommends coherence, signaling, pre-training, segmentation, modality, embodiment, and feedback principles (Mayer and colleagues) plus reflection/generative activities for self-regulation.

sections.title: Important External Factors that Influence the CAMIL
sections.summary: Names moderators outside the model proper: usability (ISO 2018), social influence/technology acceptance (Venkatesh & Davis), age, cybersickness (Munafo et al., gender-differentiated), spatial ability (Li et al. 2020), personality (Watjatrakul), absorption/predisposition (Wirth et al. 2007), and prior IVR experience/novelty.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates CAMIL as a synthesis across VR, multimedia, educational psychology, and educational technology explaining IVR's route to knowledge acquisition and transfer; calls for empirical tests of the model's paths.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: three-dimensional taxonomy (physical/social/self, after Lee 2004); driven by immersion, control factors, representational fidelity

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: one of Lee's three presence sub-dimensions; also invoked via Mayer's social agency theory for embodied agents; thinly grounded, no CMC-tradition engagement

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: defined as an objective system property (Cummings & Bailenson), distinguished terminologically from subjective presence

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: sense of generating/controlling actions (Moore & Fletcher); antecedent = control-factor fidelity via forward-modeling/CNS account (Kilteni et al.; Farrer et al.)

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: 'being inside, having, controlling a body' (Kilteni et al.); antecedents = self-presence and agency

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: grounded in Sweller's CLT and Mayer's CTML; presence AND agency both positively predict extraneous load (paths 13-14), the model's one negative-to-learning factor

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: grounded in Deci & Ryan's SDT and Pekrun's CVTAE; presence and agency both feed motivation via separate paths (7-8)

constructs.label: situational interest
constructs.treatment: Hidi & Renninger's situational/individual distinction; presence and agency both predict it (paths 5-6)

constructs.label: self-efficacy
constructs.treatment: Bandura's four efficacy sources; presence/agency framed as generating 'performance accomplishments'

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: Anderson et al. (2001) taxonomy plus transfer (Perkins & Salomon); mixed factual/conceptual findings explicitly flagged

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: IVR's most consistently reported strength per Radianti et al. (ped-sec-22)

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: presence antecedent sourced to Dalgarno & Lee (ped-sec-04, cited as '2010' — citation-year discrepancy)

constructs.label: cybersickness & physical discomfort
constructs.treatment: external moderator only, not modeled as a path; gender-differentiated per Munafo et al.

conditions.label: Makransky & Lilleholt 2018 (ped-sec-09)
conditions.role: direct empirical scaffolding — N=104 immersive-HMD vs desktop-VR crossover; source of the affective/cognitive dual-path structure CAMIL generalizes

conditions.label: Makransky & Petersen 2019 (ped-sec-11)
conditions.role: direct empirical scaffolding — N=199 desktop-VR pre/post SEM; same dual-path structure, self-efficacy terminal

conditions.label: Parong & Mayer 2018 (ped-sec-08)
conditions.role: contrasting evidence — IVR less effective than PowerPoint for factual knowledge, no difference for conceptual knowledge

conditions.label: Makransky et al. 'presence but less learning' (ped-sec-10, cited as '2019b')
conditions.role: contrasting evidence — immersive VR less effective than identical desktop simulation for declarative knowledge

conditions.label: Parong & Mayer 2020 (ped-sec-13)
conditions.role: cognitive-load evidentiary base — cited with Moreno & Mayer 2002 for IVR's higher extraneous load

conditions.label: Radianti et al. 2020 (ped-sec-22)
conditions.role: motivating review — theory-gap diagnosis; also source for IVR's procedural-knowledge strength claim

conditions.label: Meyer et al. 2019 (not in cluster)
conditions.role: N=118, pre-training principle x IVR/video 2x2, positive interaction — CAMIL's own 'media interacts with method' warrant

conditions.label: Makransky et al. 2020a (not in cluster)
conditions.role: N=165 high-schoolers, generative enactment x IVR/video 2x2, positive interaction

conditions.label: Klingenberg et al. 2020 (not in cluster)
conditions.role: N=89 biochemistry undergraduates, generative teaching x IVR/desktop-VR 2x2, positive interaction

conditions.label: Lee, Wong & Fung 2010 (not in cluster)
conditions.role: earlier desktop-VR causal framework CAMIL and its two direct SEM predecessors build on

readings.claim: The IVR-learning literature lacks an organizing theory; CAMIL is offered as that theory.
Media interacts with method: methods validated on less-immersive media generalize to IVR, but specific methods become more effective in IVR by facilitating presence/agency.
Presence and agency are IVR's two general psychological affordances, arising respectively from immersion/control/fidelity and control-factor fidelity.
Presence and agency both positively predict extraneous cognitive load, the model's sole factor with a negative path to learning outcomes.
Self-regulation's path direction (positive or negative) is contingent on instructional design rather than fixed, unlike every other path in the model.
Future research should abandon media-comparison designs in favor of interaction-focused designs testing media-by-method interactions.
Seven external factors (usability, social influence/TAM, age, cybersickness, spatial ability, personality, absorption/novelty) moderate but sit outside the model proper.

concepts.term: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
cognitive path (presence/agency -> extraneous cognitive load -> outcomes, negative)
external factors (usability, TAM, cybersickness, spatial ability, personality, absorption, novelty)

tensions.axis: Clark's 'mere vehicles' (media has no effect) vs. McLuhan's 'medium is the message' vs. CAMIL's 'media interacts with method'
tensions.note: CAMIL positions itself as a third way, structurally closer to a qualified Kozma than to either pole; this is CAMIL's own direct intervention into this cluster's debate-axis 2.

tensions.axis: affective route (presence -> enjoyment/motivation -> learning) vs. cognitive-load route (presence/agency -> extraneous load -> less learning)
tensions.note: CAMIL structurally contains both poles of this cluster's debate-axis 4 as simultaneous, non-exclusive paths from the same antecedents rather than resolving the opposition (P/anticipatory-application).

tensions.axis: self-regulation's path direction: presence/agency support reflection vs. presence/agency foreclose reflection
tensions.note: The one path in CAMIL whose sign the authors leave explicitly contingent on instructional design rather than fixed a priori.
